entities.summary:
August Heinrich Hermann von Dönhoff was a Prussian diplomat.

 Born in the late 18th century to a noble family, August Heinrich Hermann von Dönhoff served as an envoy to various European courts, including those of Russia and France. His diplomatic career spanned several decades, during which he played a key role in shaping Prussia's foreign policy.

 Von Dönhoff's tenure as ambassador to St. Petersburg from 1861 until his death in 1874 marked a pivotal moment in modern European history. He was instrumental in negotiating the Franco-Prussian War resolution of 1870, which significantly altered the balance of power in Europe and paved the way for Prussia's ascension to dominance.

 The lasting impact of von Dönhoff's diplomatic efforts can be seen in the eventual unification of Germany under Prussian leadership, a development that reshaped the European political landscape. His legacy as a skilled diplomat and statesman continues to fascinate historians and scholars today.

entities.summary:
August Heinrich Hermann von Dönhoff (1797–1874) was a prominent Prussian aristocrat and diplomat whose career spanned the tumultuous decades leading up to and immediately following the 1848 Revolutions. Born into the ancient and influential Dönhoff family in Potsdam, he embodied the traditional Junker class adapting to an era of burgeoning nationalism and liberal demands. His diplomatic postings, particularly as envoy to St. Petersburg, placed him at the heart of European power politics, shaping Prussia's foreign relations with key imperial powers during a period of shifting alliances and conservative reaction against revolutionary currents.

Educated at the Universities of Königsberg and Heidelberg, Dönhoff entered the Prussian diplomatic service in 1821. His early career saw him serve as Secretary of Legation in Stockholm (1821), London (1823), and Madrid (1825), before ascending to the rank of envoy in Madrid (1828) and Munich (1832). His most significant diplomatic appointment came in 1837 as Prussian envoy to St. Petersburg, a post he held until 1842, where he navigated complex relations with the Russian Empire under Nicholas I, a crucial partner in the Holy Alliance. In 1848, amidst the revolutionary fervor, he briefly served as Prussia's Foreign Minister under Ludolf Camphausen, advocating for a cautious, constitutional path forward before resigning after just one month.

His influence, though not world-changing, was instrumental in shaping Prussia's regional role and its response to the 1848 revolutions.
